Paragraph A
A white-crowned sparrow singing on one side of a bay does not sound quite like a white-crowned sparrow singing on the other. The species is the same and the general shape of the song is the same, but the closing phrases differ in a way that is consistent within each area and reliable enough that a trained listener can say where a bird was raised. Ornithologists borrowed a word from human speech for the phenomenon and called them dialects, and the borrowing turned out to be more apt than anyone first intended.

Paragraph B
Only a minority of birds sing in this sense. Of roughly ten thousand species, the ability to learn a song rather than inherit it whole appears in three groups: the songbirds, the parrots and the hummingbirds. Everything else is born already knowing what it will say. A flycatcher raised in complete silence still produces the correct call of its species, whereas a songbird raised the same way produces something ragged and abnormal that no female will approach. The difference is not one of intelligence but of development, and it makes the singing birds unusually useful to anyone interested in how learning works.

Paragraph C
The learning happens in two separated stages. In its first weeks a young male listens and memorises, storing a model of the song without producing anything like it. Some months later, often after a winter, he begins to practise. The early attempts are formless — researchers call this subsong, and it resembles nothing so much as a human infant babbling — and over several weeks the output is gradually adjusted until it matches the stored model. What makes this possible is that the bird can hear himself. A young bird deafened before the practice stage never converges on a normal song, even though he memorised a perfectly good one earlier.

Paragraph D
The memorising stage does not stay open. In many species the window closes after a few months, and a song heard afterwards has little effect; the adult sings for the rest of his life a version of what he took in as a juvenile. But the rule is not universal. Canaries and starlings continue to add material as adults, and a mockingbird accumulates imitations for years. The species that shut the window early and those that leave it open are not otherwise obviously different, and why the two strategies persist side by side is still argued over.

Paragraph E
Dialects arise naturally from this arrangement. If a young bird copies neighbours he can hear, and if he later settles near where he was raised, then small variations are inherited socially and reinforced locally, and boundaries appear wherever the flow of young birds is interrupted. Some boundaries follow a ridge or a river; others follow nothing visible at all. Playback experiments show that the birds themselves attend to the difference: a male responds far more aggressively to a recording in his own dialect, evidently treating a foreign singer as a less serious rival.

Paragraph F
The function of all this singing is narrower than it sounds. A song is not conversation. It advertises to females and warns off males, and in most temperate species it is produced almost exclusively by males in the breeding season. What varies is how much a female appears to care. In some species she prefers a large repertoire, in others a locally correct one, and in a few she seems indifferent to both. Since a bird's song reflects where and how well he grew up, one long-standing suggestion is that it works as an honest signal of a good start in life, though the evidence differs from species to species.

Paragraph G
A more recent finding is that birds adjust to noise. In cities, species that sing at low frequencies overlap with the roar of traffic and are simply drowned out, and populations in noisy districts have been recorded singing higher, louder, and at quieter hours than birds of the same species a few kilometres away. Whether each individual is making an adjustment or whether the noisy sites are simply occupied by higher-pitched birds is not always clear, and both explanations may be right in different places.

Paragraph H
The analogy with human language should not be pushed too far. Birdsong carries no meaning that can be recombined; a bird cannot use his song to refer to a hawk, a berry or yesterday, and no bird invents a new phrase to describe something new. What the two systems share is the mechanism rather than the product: a critical period, a stored model, a long clumsy practice phase, the need to hear oneself, and a result that varies by region because it was learnt from the neighbours. That is a narrow overlap, but it is the reason a small brown bird has taught researchers as much about learning as any laboratory animal.

(Glossary: ornithologist: a scientist who studies birds; repertoire: the full set of song types an individual can produce; playback experiment: a study in which recorded sound is played to a wild animal to observe its reaction.)
